claims.text: In single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys, strength is primarily governed by atomic lattice distortion arising from local atomic-size mismatch.
In single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys, deformation behavior is primarily governed by atomic lattice distortion arising from local atomic-size mismatch.
Greater atomic-size mismatch produces larger local lattice strain fields.
Local lattice strain fields impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy strength.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch can alter alloy failure mechanisms.
Introducing elements spanning a broader range of atomic radii increases atomic-size mismatch.
Local lattice distortion and strain can be quantified using high-resolution TEM imaging and/or XRD peak-broadening analysis.
Severe local lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation glide.
The higher-mismatch alloy will have higher yield strength than the lower-mismatch baseline alloy.
The higher-mismatch alloy will have lower dislocation mobility than the lower-mismatch baseline alloy.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch may change strain-hardening behavior.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at room temperature and potentially at temperatures below approximately 400 °C when the single phase remains stable.
Segregation, precipitation, significant local chemical ordering, or thermally activated additional mechanisms would limit the applicability of the proposed size-mismatch mechanism.
Local chemical ordering and processing-induced defects may also influence yield strength and deformation behavior.
The quantitative relationship between atomic-size mismatch and yield strength is uncertain.
